options: Every log entry on the system from every service
Only the log entries belonging to the nb-sync unit
The contents of the nb-sync systemd unit file
A list of all users currently logged in
questions.explain: The -u flag filters journalctl's output to entries logged by the named unit, matching the same unit name used with systemctl.

questions.q: What does `journalctl -u nb-sync -f` do differently from a plain `journalctl -u nb-sync`?
options: It shows only error-level entries
It follows new log entries live as they're written, instead of just showing past entries once
It filters to only the current boot
It deletes old log entries after displaying them
questions.explain: -f ('follow') behaves like tail -f, streaming new entries as they arrive rather than printing a static snapshot.

questions.q: What does `journalctl -u nginx -p err` filter for?
options: Only entries logged in the last error (the single most recent one)
Entries at error severity and anything more severe
Entries written by a user named 'err'
Only entries written before the service errored
questions.explain: -p sets a minimum priority level using standard syslog severities; it shows that level and everything more severe (e.g., crit, alert, emerg also appear when filtering at err).

options: Logs from exactly one minute ago
Logs from the previous boot, rather than the current one
Logs from the first boot the system ever had
Logs filtered to boot-related services only
questions.explain: -b selects a specific boot's logs; -1 means one boot before the current one, useful for diagnosing a crash that happened just before a reboot.

questions.q: Why might `journalctl -u nginx` still show gaps compared to what nginx actually logged?
options: journalctl always shows 100% of every service's output with no exceptions
nginx, by default, writes its access and error logs as flat files under /var/log/nginx/ rather than exclusively through journald
nginx cannot be monitored with journalctl under any configuration
journalctl only works for services written in C
questions.explain: Not every service routes its own application logging through journald — nginx typically writes directly to flat files like /var/log/nginx/access.log and error.log in addition to whatever systemd itself logs about the unit's lifecycle.
